personas.summary: NOT-GO as it stands, but the gap to publishable is narrow. This is the strongest-written condensation chapter I have reviewed here: the donor/acceptor framing is genuinely explanatory rather than list-based, every one of the 26 molecule assets parses in RDKit, and every mass balance I checked is exact — aldol additions conserve formula (2 x C2H4O = C4H8O2; 2 x C3H6O = C6H12O2), condensations lose exactly H2O (C4H8O2 -> C4H6O; C6H12O2 -> C6H10O; C11H16O3 -> C11H14O2), the Claisen loses exactly EtOH (2 x C4H8O2 - C2H6O = C6H10O3; C10H18O4 - C2H6O = C8H12O3), and the Robinson product SMILES is a correctly connected Wieland-Miescher skeleton with two fused six-membered rings, the alkene at the ring fusion and the enone conjugation in the right place. Ring sizes are correct everywhere I counted them except in one place, and that place blocks publication: the chapter twice claims that octane-2,7-dione closes to a seven-membered ring (3-methylcyclohept-2-enone) when the C3 enolate can reach C7 to give an essentially strain-free five-membered ring, delivering 1-acetyl-2-methylcyclopent-1-ene. That is not a debatable call — it contradicts the chapter's own stated principle that reversible steps funnel everything into the strain-free five- or six-membered closure, and the correct product is not even among the matching options, so the item has no defensible correct answer. Beyond that, one worked count in the Robinson section enumerates five ring atoms and calls them six, the acid-catalyzed dehydration is taught and assessed as a free beta-carbocation E1 rather than the enol route the mapped McMurry chapter gives, one distractor is labelled with a name no molecule can have, and the Robinson retrosynthesis item promises a target structure it never shows. Assessment breadth is excellent (52 items, 15 types, every concept covered by at least two types), but three learning objectives are never assessed and the entire mechanistic story is text-only because all five mechanism videos are deferred and hidden. Fix the octane-2,7-dione items and I would assign this chapter.

location.anchor_text: Octane-2,7-dione

findings.observation: The matching item keys octane-2,7-dione (l3) to 3-methylcyclohept-2-enone (r3). Octane-2,7-dione is CH3-C2(=O)-C3H2-C4H2-C5H2-C6H2-C7(=O)-CH3. Its alpha carbons are C1, C3, C6 and C8. The keyed pathway uses the C1 enolate attacking C7, which encloses seven atoms; but the C3 enolate attacking C7 encloses only five (C3-C4-C5-C6-C7), and by symmetry so does C6 attacking C2. The five-membered closure is enormously faster and is not reverted, because the resulting ketol still dehydrates: the OH sits on C7 and C3 is alpha to the surviving exocyclic acetyl group, so E1cb gives the C3=C7 alkene conjugated with that acetyl. The observed product is 1-acetyl-2-methylcyclopent-1-ene (SMILES CC(=O)C1=C(C)CCC1, C8H12O), not the keyed seven-membered enone (C8H12O). Both are C8H12O, so the item's own level-3 hint about counting ring members cannot rescue it. The correct product is not among the four options, so l3 has no defensible answer; a student who reasons correctly is forced into the wrong pairing by elimination and learns a false rule.
findings.learner_impact: Every student who works this item is taught, and graded as correct for believing, that a 1,6-diketone prefers a seven-membered aldol closure. That directly overwrites the chapter's own (correct) ring-size heuristic and will produce wrong answers on any exam question involving 2,7-diketones or 1,6-dicarbonyl retrosynthesis. Strong students who get the right chemistry will be marked wrong or will be forced by the matching constraint into an answer they know is false, which corrodes trust in the item bank.
findings.evidence: student_config.left l3 = 'Octane-2,7-dione'; student_config.right r3 = '3-Methylcyclohept-2-enone', structure_smiles 'CC1=CC(=O)CCCC1' (RDKit: C8H12O, ring sizes [7]); answer_key.correct_pairs l3 -> r3. Contrast the chapter's own rule in nugget-intramolecular-aldol: 'Any closure that would give a three- or four-membered ring is strained and simply comes back apart faster than it goes on. Only the closure to an unstrained five- or six-membered ring survives long enough to dehydrate.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs this item to test only substrates whose favoured closure is unambiguous, and it needs the 1,6-diketone case either removed or re-keyed to the five-membered outcome with the correct product structure present as an option. If the authors want to keep a 1,6-diketone, the chapter also needs an explicit statement of what happens when both a five-ring and a larger ring are geometrically reachable, since that is exactly the discrimination the item is currently mis-teaching.

location.anchor_text: The isolated product is the cyclic conjugated enone after dehydration, 3-methylcyclohept-2-enone

findings.observation: The section's practice_check asks what octane-2,7-dione gives with NaOH and answers that the C1 enolate attacks C7 to enclose a seven-membered ring, giving 3-methylcyclohept-2-enone, hedged only with 'seven-membered rings close far less readily than five- and six-membered ones, so yields are correspondingly lower'. This is the same error as inst-001 and is worse here because it is presented as the section's own worked reasoning. The hedge is precisely backwards: the reason seven-membered closure is slow is exactly why the competing five-membered closure (C3 enolate onto C7) takes over completely. The answer also mis-labels the substrate: it calls carbonyls at C2 and C7 'a 1,6-diketone relationship' while the chapter's own convention elsewhere counts positions (hexane-2,5-dione is called a 1,4-diketone), so the labelling is internally consistent but the conclusion drawn from it is not.
findings.learner_impact: This is the retrieval item a student uses to self-check immediately after reading the ring-size rule. It teaches an incorrect product and, more damagingly, teaches a wrong method: extrapolate the chain-length rule linearly instead of asking which reachable closure is strain-free. Students will carry this into Robinson retrosynthesis, where recognising the five-ring alternative matters.
findings.evidence: nuggets[4].practice_check.answer: 'The enolate at carbon one attacks the carbonyl at carbon seven, enclosing carbons one through seven: a seven-membered ring. The isolated product is the cyclic conjugated enone after dehydration, 3-methylcyclohept-2-enone.' RDKit confirms both candidate products are C8H12O; the five-membered candidate CC(=O)C1=C(C)CCC1 has ring sizes [5].
findings.recommended_outcome: The section needs a practice item whose substrate has an unambiguous favoured closure, and the chapter needs the missing generalisation — that when two ring sizes are reachable the five- or six-membered one wins regardless of which enolate is drawn first — stated explicitly rather than left to be inferred from the 1,4/1,5 pair.

location.anchor_text: the attacking carbon, the two CH₂ groups, the quaternary carbon, and the carbonyl carbon under attack — six, so a six-membered ring

findings.observation: The expanded text's atom-by-atom count of the new Robinson ring enumerates five atoms and then asserts six. The side chain installed by the Michael stage is -CH2-CH2-C(=O)-CH3; the ring formed when the terminal methyl attacks a ring carbonyl is [attacking CH2] + [side-chain ketone carbon] + [two CH2 groups] + [quaternary carbon] + [attacked carbonyl carbon] = six. The list omits the side-chain ketone carbon, which is precisely the carbon that becomes the enone carbonyl of the new ring. The product SMILES CC12CCC(=O)C=C1CCCC2=O is correct and does place that carbonyl inside the new six-membered ring, so the structure and the conclusion are right and only the enumeration is wrong — but this is the chapter's single most important worked count.
findings.learner_impact: A student following along literally counts five and concludes either that they have mis-drawn the intermediate or that the ring is five-membered. Worse, the omitted atom is the one whose fate they most need to track: a student who leaves the side-chain ketone carbon outside the ring will place the surviving carbonyl on the wrong side and draw a bicyclic diketone with the enone in the old ring rather than the new one.
findings.evidence: nuggets[9].text.expanded: 'In the aldol stage the terminal methyl of that chain is deprotonated and attacks one of the two ring carbonyls. Count the atoms enclosed: the attacking carbon, the two CH₂ groups, the quaternary carbon, and the carbonyl carbon under attack — six, so a six-membered ring.' Compare mol-wieland-miescher-ketone SMILES CC12CCC(=O)C=C1CCCC2=O, RDKit ring sizes [6, 6], with the conjugated ketone inside the newly formed ring.
findings.recommended_outcome: The Robinson worked example needs its ring-atom enumeration to name all six atoms in order, and needs the side-chain carbonyl carbon explicitly identified as the carbon that becomes the new ring's ketone, since that identification is what makes the subsequent dehydration and the retrosynthetic disconnection legible.

location.anchor_text: a proton goes onto the hydroxyl oxygen, water departs to leave a carbocation at the beta carbon, and an alpha proton is then lost to give the alkene

findings.observation: The chapter presents acid-catalyzed dehydration of an aldol as a clean E1 through a discrete carbocation at the beta carbon, and then assesses that model as categorically true in an advanced comparison matrix (feature f_cation, 'Passes through a carbocation at the beta carbon', keyed 'Applies' for the acid case). The mapped textbook (OpenStax/McMurry ch. 23) routes acid-catalyzed dehydration through the enol: the carbonyl is protonated, the enol forms, the hydroxyl is then protonated and water leaves with the enol pi bond assisting. The chapter's running dehydration example is 3-hydroxybutanal, whose beta carbon is secondary; a free secondary carbocation is not a defensible intermediate here. The E1 picture is only reasonable for the tertiary case (4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one), which the chapter never distinguishes.
findings.learner_impact: Students are given a mechanism they will be told is wrong in the next course, and are graded on it as an either/or matrix cell with no room to answer correctly. It also teaches a false symmetry ('the mirror-image route') that hides the real point: both catalysts work by first generating a nucleophilic carbon (enolate or enol) adjacent to the leaving group, which is why beta-hydroxy carbonyls dehydrate when ordinary alcohols do not.
findings.evidence: nuggets[2].text.expanded: 'Acid catalysis reaches the same product by the mirror-image route: a proton goes onto the hydroxyl oxygen, water departs to leave a carbocation at the beta carbon, and an alpha proton is then lost to give the alkene.' ch23-addition-vs-dehydration-v2 answer_key [redacted] and f_carbanion = {case_base: 'yes', case_acid: 'no'}; the chapter's dehydration examples are 3-hydroxybutanal (secondary beta carbon) and 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one (tertiary).
findings.recommended_outcome: The acid-catalyzed route needs to be described as the mapped textbook describes it — enolization first, then loss of protonated water assisted by the enol — or, if a simplified E1 is retained deliberately, it needs to be scoped to substrates with a tertiary beta carbon and the assessment item needs to stop asserting a free beta carbocation as a general truth.

location.anchor_text: 4-Methylpentane-2,4-dione

findings.observation: Distractor option d is labelled '4-Methylpentane-2,4-dione' but carries structure_smiles CC(=O)CC(C)=O, which RDKit resolves to C5H8O2 — pentane-2,4-dione (acetylacetone). The displayed name is not merely a mismatch; it names a molecule that cannot exist, since C4 would need a ketone oxygen, a methyl, C3 and C5 (five bonds). The paired wrong-answer explanation compounds the problem: it says the compound 'has lost two hydrogens rather than a molecule of water', but relative to the C6H12O2 starting material this structure has lost CH4, not H2. The explanation's second clause ('one carbon fewer') is correct and contradicts its own first clause.
findings.learner_impact: Students see a rendered structure captioned with an impossible IUPAC name and an explanation whose stated bookkeeping does not match either the name or the structure. Students who are learning to use formula bookkeeping as their check — which this very question's level-1 hint tells them to do — get a worked comparison that fails their own check, and some will conclude their formula arithmetic is unreliable.
findings.evidence: ch23-dehydration-product-v2 student_config.options[3] = {text: '4-Methylpentane-2,4-dione', structure_smiles: 'CC(=O)CC(C)=O'}; RDKit formula C5H8O2, canonical CC(=O)CC(C)=O = pentane-2,4-dione. Starting material CC(=O)CC(C)(C)O = C6H12O2. feedback_bundle wrong_answer_explanations option_id d: 'This compound has lost two hydrogens rather than a molecule of water, and it has one carbon fewer than the starting material.'
findings.recommended_outcome: This distractor needs a name that matches the structure it renders and an explanation whose atom bookkeeping is arithmetically true. More usefully, the distractor set needs a fourth option that is a genuine isomer of the substrate or of the correct product, so the formula check the hints teach actually discriminates.

location.anchor_text: A target cyclohexenone is to be traced back to the two compounds that would build it

findings.observation: This advanced structured_reasoning item opens by referring to 'a target cyclohexenone' and asks the student to trace it back to its Michael donor and acceptor, but student_config contains only a fields array — no start_structure, no target_structure, no structure_smiles anywhere in the item. There is no target to analyse. The accessibility_bundle repeats the promise ('A target cyclohexenone is to be analysed retrosynthetically') without supplying one. The three fields happen to be answerable generically, which is precisely the problem: the item is billed as a retrosynthesis of a specific compound and is in fact a definitional recall item.
findings.learner_impact: Students hunt for a structure that is not there and either report the question as broken or, more often, guess. The item also fails to assess the objective it is the only candidate for — 'Work backward from a cyclohexenone product to the donor and acceptor that would build it' — because no product is ever presented. Nothing in the chapter's 52 items requires a student to actually perform a Robinson disconnection on a structure.
findings.evidence: ch23-robinson-retrosynthesis student_config keys = ['fields'] only; no structure_smiles appears anywhere in the item (verified by exhaustive walk over the question for smiles/structure_smiles/molecule_smiles keys). Compare ch23-robinson-route, which does supply start_structure and target_structure with SMILES. nuggets[9].learning_objectives[2] = 'Work backward from a cyclohexenone product to the donor and acceptor that would build it.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The item needs the target compound it references to be present and inspectable, and the chapter needs at least one item in which a student performs the three disconnections on an actual structure rather than only naming their order.

location.anchor_text: but whose climb measured from the valley immediately before it is smaller than the first climb measured from the start

findings.observation: Both reaction_coordinate_reasoning items ask for rate_determining_step, and both accessible_descriptions state the barrier comparison outright rather than describing the curve's geometry. In the first item the description says the second maximum's 'climb measured from the valley immediately before it is smaller than the first climb measured from the start'; in the variant it says the second climb 'is larger than the first climb measured from the start'. A sighted student must derive that comparison from the plotted heights; a screen-reader student is handed it. This is the same leak class the previous chapter's review identified: the accessible description may give relative heights but must not state the derived quantity that the ask is asking for.
findings.learner_impact: The item stops assessing the skill it exists to assess for exactly the learners who most need it assessed. It also creates a differential grading advantage and, in the other direction, denies those learners the practice of measuring a barrier from its own preceding valley — which is the misconception the generic_incorrect_explanation says the item is designed to correct.
findings.evidence: ch23-aldol-dehydration-profile accessibility_bundle.accessible_description and ch23-aldol-dehydration-profile-v2 accessible_description, both compared against student_config.ask = ['step_count','rate_determining_step','overall','step_types']. The underlying keys are chemically correct (v1: barriers 18 vs 16, RDS = step 1; v2: barriers 15 vs 18, RDS = step 2).
findings.recommended_outcome: These two descriptions need to convey only what the plot shows — the numeric or clearly relative height of each minimum and maximum — and leave the barrier comparison for the student to perform, so the non-visual and visual versions of the task demand the same reasoning.

location.anchor_text: The bond formed is always donor alpha carbon to acceptor carbonyl carbon

findings.observation: The chapter's organising rule is stated as exceptionless in all three depths ('the new bond is always the same one', 'The bond formed is always donor alpha carbon to acceptor carbonyl carbon; there is no version of this chemistry in which two alpha carbons bond to each other, or two carbonyl carbons do'). Two paragraphs later the same nugget introduces the Michael reaction, in which the enolate bonds to the acceptor's beta carbon and not to its carbonyl carbon. The 'always' is therefore falsified by one of the four named reactions the same nugget is previewing, and nothing signals the exception at the point the rule is asserted.
findings.learner_impact: The rule is stated in the most memorable place in the chapter and repeated three times, so it is what students will encode. They will then reach ch23-michael-attack-site and ch23-michael-arrow with a rule that predicts option c (attack at the alpha carbon adjacent to the carbonyl) or attack at the carbonyl carbon, and be told they are wrong by a chapter that told them the rule admits no exceptions. The Michael section's own trouble_spot anticipates exactly this error but the intro nugget causes it.
findings.evidence: nuggets[0].text.standard: 'the new bond is always the same one: donor alpha carbon to acceptor carbonyl carbon'; nuggets[0].text.expanded: 'there is no version of this chemistry in which two alpha carbons bond to each other, or two carbonyl carbons do'; the same expanded text then states 'the enolate can attack the far end of that alkene instead of the carbonyl carbon — that is the Michael reaction.' concepts[7].trouble_spots[0]: 'Sending the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon: a stabilized, reversible nucleophile ends up on the beta carbon.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The organising rule needs to be scoped where it is first asserted — the donor always supplies its alpha carbon, but the acceptor supplies either its carbonyl carbon or, when conjugated, its beta carbon — so that the Michael reaction reads as a case of the pattern rather than a contradiction of it.

location.anchor_text: Highly reactive, non-stabilized nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents and hydride donors attack the carbonyl carbon directly, giving 1,2-addition

findings.observation: The 1,2- versus 1,4- decision is presented as fully determined by nucleophile reactivity, with organometallics and hydrides assigned unconditionally to 1,2-addition. The chapter never mentions organocuprates, which are organometallic and give clean 1,4-addition, nor that NaBH4 on an enone gives substantial conjugate reduction (the reason Luche conditions exist). The words 'cuprate' and 'Gilman' do not appear anywhere in the package. The reversibility argument the chapter gives is sound as far as it goes but is presented as the whole story.
findings.learner_impact: Students form a hard rule — organometallic means 1,2 — that has to be un-taught the moment cuprates appear, and they lose the more durable idea that hard/soft character and reversibility, not simply 'reactive versus stabilized', decide the site. A student asked on a later exam to add a methyl group to the beta carbon of an enone will reach for a Grignard.
findings.evidence: nuggets[7].text.standard: 'Highly reactive, non-stabilized nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents and hydride donors attack the carbonyl carbon directly, giving 1,2-addition.' nuggets[7].text.expanded: 'A Grignard reagent or a hydride donor is highly reactive and its addition to a carbonyl is effectively irreversible; it attacks the nearest and most electrophilic site, the carbonyl carbon, and stays there.' grep for 'cuprate' and 'Gilman' in the package returns 0 hits.
findings.recommended_outcome: The section needs at least a one-sentence acknowledgement that some organometallics (notably diorganocuprates) deliver carbon to the beta carbon, so that the rule is framed as a strong tendency with a named counterexample rather than as a law; without it the chapter builds a misconception it will have to spend later chapters removing.

findings.observation: Two of the three learning objectives for this concept are never assessed. LO2 asks students to 'Predict a single product when one partner cannot enolize, and identify which partner supplies the alpha carbon', and LO3 asks them to 'Recognize the second selectivity strategy, in which a much more acidic donor monopolizes the donor role'. The concept's four items are two numeric product counts and two multi-selects that only classify compounds as enolizable or not. No item in the entire chapter asks a student to produce or select a crossed aldol product — not even benzaldehyde plus acetone, for which an asset (mol-benzalacetone) already exists — and no item on this concept touches the acidity strategy. The mixed Claisen partners the prose introduces (ethyl formate, ethyl benzoate, diethyl carbonate, diethyl oxalate) are likewise never assessed as acceptors.
findings.learner_impact: Students can pass every item on the most synthetically important selectivity section by doing structure triage alone, without ever drawing a crossed product or reasoning about which of two partners donates. The section's central practical skill — predict the one product a well-designed mixed condensation gives — is taught and then never practised, so an instructor assigning this bank cannot tell whether it has landed.
findings.evidence: nuggets[3].learning_objectives vs the four items keyed to concept_slug 'mixed-aldol-selectivity': ch23-mixed-aldol-product-count (answer 4), ch23-mixed-aldol-product-count-v2 (answer 2), ch23-clean-mixed-aldol-partners (a,b,e), ch23-clean-mixed-aldol-partners-v2 (a,c,e). Asset mol-benzalacetone exists with the Claisen-Schmidt product and is used by no question.
findings.recommended_outcome: This concept needs practice that requires producing a crossed-aldol product structure and naming which partner supplied the alpha carbon, and it needs at least one item exercising the acidity-based selectivity strategy so both taught routes to a clean mixed condensation are assessed.

location.anchor_text: Use the reversibility of the reaction to predict the fragments of a retro-aldol cleavage.

findings.observation: The retro-aldol is developed at length — it is a stated learning objective, a concept trouble_spot, the subject of the section's practice_check, and the biological hook (aldolase cleaving fructose 1,6-bisphosphate) — but none of the eight items keyed to aldol-reaction assess it. All eight run the reaction forward: two product single-selects, two forward drawings, two forward bond ledgers, two forward attack arrows. The same gap exists for dieckmann-cyclization LO3 ('Connect the cyclic product to the alkylation and decarboxylation chemistry of beta-keto esters'), which no item touches.
findings.learner_impact: Retro-aldol disconnection is the highest-transfer skill in the section — it is the retrosynthetic move the chapter itself calls 'one of the most reliable retrosynthetic disconnections in the course' and the one that carries into biochemistry — and a student can complete every graded item without ever running a step backward. Instructors assigning this bank get no signal on whether students can reverse the reaction.
findings.evidence: nuggets[1].learning_objectives[2]; nuggets[1].text.expanded: 'this is one of the most reliable retrosynthetic disconnections in the course'; the eight aldol-reaction items are ch23-aldol-product-propanal(+v2), ch23-draw-aldol-product(+v2), ch23-aldol-bond-ledger(+v2), ch23-aldol-attack-arrow(+v2), all forward-direction. nuggets[6].learning_objectives[2] with dieckmann items ch23-dieckmann-ring-size(+v2), ch23-draw-dieckmann-product(+v2).
findings.recommended_outcome: The aldol section needs practice that runs the equilibrium backward — given a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound, identify the bond that cleaves and the two fragments — and the Dieckmann section needs an item connecting its cyclic beta-keto ester to the alkylation/decarboxylation sequence its objective promises.

location.anchor_text: video-aldol-mechanism

findings.observation: All 26 assets in this chapter are static single molecules, and all five video_briefs are production_status 'deferred'; in the compiled reader every video block carries is_hidden true and url ''. The result is that no figure anywhere in the chapter shows a bond forming, an arrow, a tetrahedral intermediate, or an energy comparison. The chapter's four hardest ideas are all comparative or dynamic — enolate attack at the carbonyl carbon versus the beta carbon, the aldol tetrahedral intermediate protonating versus the Claisen one collapsing, the coupled unfavourable-addition/irreversible-dehydration equilibrium, and the two-stage Robinson ring build — and each is carried entirely by prose. There is a reaction_coordinate_reasoning question type in use, yet no reaction-coordinate figure asset exists in the chapter at all.
findings.learner_impact: Students must hold a multi-step electron-flow story in working memory from text alone at the exact points where the chapter's own trouble_spots say they fail. The Michael regiochemistry in particular is a spatial claim ('two carbons away from the oxygen') delivered without a single picture distinguishing the two electrophilic sites, and the aldol-versus-Claisen divergence is a side-by-side comparison with no side-by-side figure.
findings.evidence: assets[] contains 26 entries, all type 'molecule'; video_briefs[0..4] all have production_status 'deferred'; compiled reader frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carbonyl-condensation.json block_type counts = {molecule: 36, text: 10, external_link: 10, video: 5, mcmurry_link: 1}, with all five video blocks is_hidden true and content.url ''. Question ch23-aldol-dehydration-profile uses a profile that exists only inside the question, not as a chapter asset.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs a non-video visual equivalent for at least the two electrophilic sites of an enone and for the aldol/Claisen tetrahedral-intermediate divergence, since those are the two claims students are graded on most and currently have no figure support of any kind; it also needs the coupled-equilibrium energy story available as a figure rather than only inside one assessment item.

location.anchor_text: practice_check

findings.observation: All ten nuggets carry a practice_check with a prompt and a worked answer, and none of them reaches the compiled reader. The compiled chapter contains only molecule, text, external_link, video and mcmurry_link blocks — there is no practice_check block type at all. The same is true of the assets' long_description fields: the reader's molecule blocks carry only alt_text and the learning_goal as 'description', so the atom-by-atom walkthroughs written for each figure (which is where the alpha/beta carbon identifications actually live) are not delivered either.
findings.learner_impact: A reader student gets ten sections of continuous exposition with zero interleaved retrieval, and must go to the separate question bank to test anything. The long_descriptions are where the chapter does its most careful atom labelling — for example mol-3-hydroxybutanal's 'The bond between carbons two and three is the new carbon-carbon bond made in the reaction' — and losing them removes the bridge between the prose and the picture at exactly the moments the prose says to trace atoms.

Reader molecule block content keys are ['name','smiles','alt_text','description','generator_href'(,'rdkit_options')] with description == the asset's learning_goal; assets[].accessibility.long_description appears nowhere in the compiled reader.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs its ten authored retrieval prompts and its per-figure atom walkthroughs to actually reach the reading surface; as compiled, a substantial fraction of the authored teaching content is written but undeliverable, which an instructor assigning the reader has no way to detect.

findings.observation: The michael-reaction concept declares only carbonyl-condensation-pattern as a prerequisite, but its nugget depends on two later concepts. It requires alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compounds, which the chapter creates in aldol-condensation-dehydration (order 3), and it leans on the pKa-versus-ethanol selectivity argument built in mixed-aldol-selectivity (order 4), which explicitly forward-references it: 'The same logic will explain the Michael reaction later in the chapter.' Robinson annulation similarly omits aldol-condensation-dehydration, though it inherits it transitively through intramolecular-aldol.
findings.learner_impact: Any surface that sequences by declared prerequisites — a concept map, an adaptive path, an instructor building a partial assignment — could place the Michael reaction before enones have been introduced, leaving the acceptor unexplained. The reading order is correct; only the machine-readable dependency graph is wrong.
findings.evidence: concepts[7].prerequisites = ['carbonyl-condensation-pattern']; nuggets[7].text.standard opens 'An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound has two electrophilic sites'; nuggets[3].text.expanded closes 'The same logic will explain the Michael reaction later in the chapter, where stabilized donors are chosen for exactly this reason.'

location.anchor_text: acetaldehyde is converted largely to its aldol

findings.observation: The chapter states that 'Aldehydes generally give good conversion; acetaldehyde is converted largely to its aldol.' The standard figure for acetaldehyde's aldol equilibrium is roughly 50 percent conversion, which supports 'favours product' but not 'largely'. The contrast the section is drawing — aldehydes favour product, ketones do not — is correct and well made; only the quantitative colouring overstates.
findings.learner_impact: Minor, but it slightly undercuts the section's own best point. The reason the aldol equilibrium matters is that it sits near the middle for aldehydes and far to the left for ketones, which is what makes the coupled irreversible dehydration such a general trick. Overstating the aldehyde case makes the ketone case look like a special deficiency rather than the same equilibrium shifted.
findings.evidence: nuggets[1].text.standard: 'Aldehydes generally give good conversion; acetaldehyde is converted largely to its aldol. Ketones do not. Acetone under the same conditions reaches equilibrium at only a few percent product'. The acetone figure (a few percent) matches the standard value; the acetaldehyde characterisation does not.
findings.recommended_outcome: The aldehyde equilibrium needs a figure or a hedge consistent with the roughly even conversion normally quoted, so that the aldehyde/ketone contrast is a matter of degree on one scale rather than an apparent success/failure dichotomy.

location.anchor_text: A successful Claisen needs at least two alpha hydrogens on the donor.

findings.observation: The two-alpha-hydrogen requirement is stated without qualification in the nugget, in the section's practice_check answer, and in the keyed repair option of ch23-flawed-claisen. The rule is exactly right for the alkoxide-mediated Claisen the chapter teaches, because the driving force is the final deprotonation. It is not a structural impossibility: with a full equivalent of a strong, non-nucleophilic base that is not regenerated as an alcohol, esters bearing a single alpha hydrogen can be condensed. The chapter's own framing already supplies the correct reasoning ('the driving step is unavailable'), so the exception is one clause away.
findings.learner_impact: Low. Students carry a rule that is operationally correct for every problem in this course but is stated as a structural law rather than a thermodynamic consequence, so a later encounter with a forced Claisen reads as a contradiction rather than as the same argument with a different base.
findings.evidence: nuggets[5].text.expanded: 'An ester with a single alpha hydrogen gives a product with none, the driving step is unavailable, and the condensation fails.' nuggets[5].practice_check.answer: 'A successful Claisen needs at least two alpha hydrogens on the donor.' ch23-flawed-claisen repair_options fix_two_h, keyed correct.
findings.recommended_outcome: The requirement needs to be attributed to the driving deprotonation rather than presented as an absolute structural bar, so that students learn a transferable thermodynamic argument rather than a rule with an unexplained exception waiting for them.

location.anchor_text: the double bond is exocyclic to the chain at carbons four and five

findings.observation: Two terminology slips. First, a wrong-answer explanation for an acyclic substrate describes its alkene as 'exocyclic to the chain' — there is no ring anywhere in 4-methylpent-4-en-2-one, and every other use of 'exocyclic' in the package (seven of eight) correctly refers to the Dieckmann product's ester group hanging off a ring. Second, the Claisen-Schmidt condensation is scoped two different ways: the standard-depth text defines it as 'an aromatic aldehyde with an enolizable ketone', while the expanded text narrows it to 'When the enolizable partner is a methyl ketone'.
findings.learner_impact: Small but real. 'Exocyclic' is a term students are actively learning to use precisely, and seeing it applied to an open chain in a graded explanation undermines that. The Claisen-Schmidt scoping difference means a student reading at two depths gets two different definitions of the same named reaction and may wrongly conclude that a non-methyl ketone does not qualify.
findings.evidence: ch23-dehydration-product-v2 feedback_bundle.wrong_answer_explanations option_id b: 'Water has been lost, but the double bond is exocyclic to the chain at carbons four and five'. nuggets[3].text.standard: 'This particular combination, an aromatic aldehyde with an enolizable ketone, is named the Claisen-Schmidt condensation'; nuggets[3].text.expanded: 'When the enolizable partner is a methyl ketone and the acceptor is an aromatic aldehyde, the reaction is called the Claisen-Schmidt condensation'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs consistent terminology for ring-attached versus chain positions, and one scope for the Claisen-Schmidt name across all three depths, so that terms the chapter is teaching students to use precisely are used precisely in the chapter's own explanations.

location.anchor_text: https://openstax.org/books/organic-chemistry/pages/23-why-this-chapter

findings.observation: The compiled reader contains exactly one OpenStax link for the whole chapter, and it points at the chapter's 'why this chapter' landing page rather than at any specific section. The ten Wikipedia links are per-concept and well chosen, but the assigned-textbook link gives a student who wants to read further on, say, the Dieckmann cyclization or conjugate addition nothing more targeted than the chapter opener.
findings.learner_impact: A student who wants the textbook's treatment of one specific reaction has to navigate the chapter themselves, and an instructor cannot point at a section-level correspondence when building an assignment. The per-concept mapping the chapter has already done internally is not exposed to the reader.

location.anchor_text: "y_axis_label": "Free energy, G"

findings.observation: Both reaction-coordinate profiles plot numeric free energies (0, 18, 4, 20, -12 and 0, 15, -6, 12, -20) against an axis labelled only 'Free energy, G' with no units. Beyond the notation issue, the acetone profile places the aldol addition product 4 units above starting material; if those units are kcal/mol that corresponds to roughly 0.1 percent product at equilibrium, whereas the chapter's prose says acetone reaches 'only a few percent' (about 1.8 kcal/mol). The relative comparisons the item actually grades are unaffected.
findings.learner_impact: Minor. Students in an advanced item are shown quantitative energies they cannot interpret, and the one number that could be checked against the chapter's own prose does not match it. A student who tries to connect the diagram to the 'few percent' figure from the aldol section will not be able to.
findings.evidence: ch23-aldol-dehydration-profile student_config.profile.control y values [0.0, 18.0, 4.0, 20.0, -12.0] with y_axis_label 'Free energy, G'; nuggets[1].text.standard: 'Acetone under the same conditions reaches equilibrium at only a few percent product'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The profiles need an explicit energy unit on the axis, and the addition-product minimum needs to be consistent with the equilibrium position the chapter states in prose, so the diagram and the text describe the same system.

strengths: Every SMILES in the package parses, and every mass balance I checked is exact: aldol additions conserve formula (2 x C2H4O = C4H8O2 for 3-hydroxybutanal; 2 x C3H6O = C6H12O2 for diacetone alcohol), condensations lose exactly one water (C4H8O2 -> C4H6O; C6H12O2 -> C6H10O; C7H12O2 -> C7H10O; C11H16O3 -> C11H14O2), the Claisen and Dieckmann lose exactly EtOH (2 x C4H8O2 - C2H6O = C6H10O3; C10H18O4 - C2H6O = C8H12O3), enamine formation loses exactly water (C6H10O + C4H9N - H2O = C10H17N), and both Michael adducts are exact sums of their partners.

The Robinson annulation product is structurally correct in a way that is easy to get wrong: CC12CCC(=O)C=C1CCCC2=O gives two fused six-membered rings sharing an edge, the quaternary methyl-bearing carbon at one fusion, the alkene at the other fusion conjugated to the newly formed ring's ketone, and the original ring's ketone adjacent to the quaternary carbon. The cyclopentane variant (Hajos-Parrish skeleton, rings [5,6]) is equally correct, as are both ketol intermediates.

The aldol/Claisen divergence is taught as one mechanism with one branch point — whether the acceptor's tetrahedral intermediate has a leaving group — rather than as two reactions to memorise. This is the single most useful reorganisation in the chapter and it is sustained across prose, the comparison_matrix item, and the video brief.

The pKa scale is used quantitatively and consistently everywhere it appears (2,4-pentanedione 9, beta-keto ester 11, malonate 13, ethanol 16, ketone 19, ester 25), and the chapter draws the right structural conclusion from it — that ethanol at 16 is the dividing line that determines which partner monopolises the donor role. The rank_order item, the Claisen driving-force item, and the Robinson donor-selection item all key against the same scale.

Assessment breadth is genuinely strong: 52 items across 15 types with 26 surfaced plus 26 variants, every concept covered by at least two different types, and no concept assessed only by a drawing task. Distractors are mostly principled — the alpha-attack isomer, the 1,2-addition alcohol, the condensation product where addition was asked — and RDKit confirms the key distractors in the aldol and Michael items are true isomers of the correct answer, so formula-counting alone cannot solve them.

The intramolecular aldol and Dieckmann worked examples both number the chain explicitly and count ring atoms correctly, and the Dieckmann section pre-empts the standard off-by-one error by naming exactly which carbon ends up exocyclic.
open_questions: inst-004 (acid-catalyzed dehydration via a beta carbocation) is the one finding where I could see an instructor disagreeing about severity. The E1 picture is defensible for the chapter's tertiary example (4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one) but not for its primary example (3-hydroxybutanal, secondary beta carbon), and it contradicts the enol route given by the mapped OpenStax/McMurry chapter 23. I scored it high rather than blocker; if the project's standard is strict alignment with the mapped text, it should be promoted to a publication blocker.

inst-007 (the reaction-coordinate accessible_description stating the barrier comparison) meets the letter of the 'leaked answer' blocker definition for screen-reader users specifically. I scored it high rather than blocker because the leak is one sub-answer of four and because any faithful description must convey relative heights. The accessibility persona may reasonably escalate it; I would defer to that call.

Is the missing practice_check and long_description delivery in the compiled reader (inst-013) a chapter-authoring defect or the known platform gap carried over from the two preceding chapters? If platform, the finding should be routed to the pipeline rather than to a content revision, but the chapter still ships with a large fraction of its authored teaching text undeliverable and an instructor should be told that before assigning the reader.

The Wieland-Miescher ketone is never named in prose (asset id mol-wieland-miescher-ketone, title 'The bicyclic enone from the Robinson annulation') and is drawn without stereochemistry. Racemic is correct for the base-mediated reaction taught here, so I did not raise a finding, but if a later chapter covers proline-catalysed asymmetric annulation the authors may want the name introduced here as a hook.

I did not find a second-defensible-answer problem anywhere except the octane-2,7-dione case: all four diketones in each matching item are symmetric, and I verified by enumerating every alpha-carbon-to-carbonyl closure for each substrate that only the octane-2,7-dione entry admits a competing favoured ring size.

personas.summary: The chemistry here is careful and the wrong-answer explanations are among the best I have read in this course — most distractors are diagnosed by name, and three of the four ring-counting worked examples walk atom by atom. But the chapter is delivered as ten walls of prose with every structure parked after the text, zero mechanism figures, zero delivered practice checks, and five mechanism animations that ship with empty URLs and is_hidden set. Every intermediate the chapter's central argument turns on — the tetrahedral intermediate, the alkoxide, the carbinolamine, the iminium — is described in words and never drawn. Worse, the reader defaults to the 'expanded' detail level, and several definitions I actually need (what 'condensation' means, what 'aldol' means, the addition-versus-condensation naming rule that four graded questions hinge on, what 'annulation' means, and the Dieckmann off-by-one warning) exist only in the 'standard' variant, which I would have to guess to go looking for. The capstone Robinson worked example lists five atoms and calls the count six. Two advanced free-energy-profile questions assume a skill the chapter never touches — the prose contains no energy diagram and never uses the words transition state, barrier, or rate-determining step — and one of them reports two steps for a reaction the prose says has three. As a shaky student I could follow individual sentences all day and still stall at exactly the places I would be graded.

location.anchor_text: When a sequence includes this dehydration it is called an aldol condensation, reserving aldol reaction or aldol addition for the case that stops at the alcohol.

findings.observation: The reader renders one detail level at a time and defaults to 'expanded' ([internal source reference — not in this repo] sets detailLevel: "expanded"; TopicPackageChapterRenderer swaps content.markdown for _detail_texts[prefs.detailLevel]). The levels are alternatives, not cumulative, and several load-bearing definitions exist ONLY in the 'standard' variant and appear nowhere in the 'expanded' text that is actually shown by default: why the reaction is called a condensation, where the word 'aldol' comes from, the rule that 'aldol condensation' means the sequence including dehydration while 'aldol reaction'/'aldol addition' means stopping at the alcohol, and that 'annulation means ring building'.
findings.learner_impact: I open the chapter, get the densest of the three texts by default, and never learn what the chapter's four central words mean. Then I hit ch23-draw-aldol-product ('Draw the aldol addition product'), ch23-aldol-product-propanal ('Which structure is the aldol addition product?') and ch23-dehydration-product ('Which structure is the condensation product?') and I have no basis at all for telling addition from condensation. I guess, get it wrong, read a feedback line that says 'The question asks for the addition product' as if I should have known, and conclude I am not smart enough for this chapter.
findings.evidence: _detail_texts.standard of nugget-aldol-condensation-dehydration contains the addition-vs-condensation naming rule; the rendered blk-59t2y57n markdown (= _detail_texts.expanded) never uses the phrase 'aldol condensation' at all. _detail_texts.standard of nugget-carbonyl-condensation-pattern contains 'Because two carbonyl-containing molecules are joined, the reaction is called a condensation'; expanded does not. _detail_texts.standard of nugget-aldol-reaction contains 'which is where the name aldol comes from'; expanded does not. _detail_texts.standard of nugget-robinson-annulation opens 'Annulation means ring building'; expanded does not. Affected surfaced questions: ch23-draw-aldol-product, ch23-aldol-product-propanal, ch23-dehydration-product, ch23-intramolecular-ring-product.
findings.recommended_outcome: Every term the chapter grades on must be defined at whatever detail level the student is reading, including the default one; the terminology that separates 'addition' from 'condensation' cannot live in a variant a struggling reader has no reason to switch to.

location.anchor_text: Count the atoms enclosed: the attacking carbon, the two CH₂ groups, the quaternary carbon, and the carbonyl carbon under attack — six, so a six-membered ring.

findings.observation: In the chapter's single atom-by-atom walkthrough of the capstone reaction, the enumerated list contains five atoms (attacking carbon + two CH₂ + quaternary carbon + attacked carbonyl carbon) but is asserted to be six. The side-chain ketone carbon, which sits between the attacking methyl and the CH₂CH₂ linker and IS a member of the new ring, is omitted from the list. The stated conclusion (six-membered) is correct; the count-along is not.
findings.learner_impact: The chapter has just spent three earlier sections training me to count ring atoms by listing them (and the intramolecular-aldol and Dieckmann sections do it correctly). So I count along, get five, and conclude either that the ring is five-membered or — far more likely for me — that I have misunderstood something fundamental about which atoms are in a ring. I stop and reread the paragraph three times, then give up on the Robinson section entirely, which is also the section the two synthesis_route questions and both structured_reasoning questions are built on.
findings.evidence: blk-venwqh8r markdown, paragraph 4. The correct ring for 2-methyl-2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexane-1,3-dione closing to CC12CCC(=O)C=C1CCCC2=O is: attacking CH₂, side-chain ketone carbon, CH₂, CH₂, quaternary carbon, attacked ring carbonyl carbon = six. Compare the correct enumerations in nugget-intramolecular-aldol ('carbons one, two, three, four, and five — a five-membered ring') and nugget-dieckmann-cyclization ('encloses carbons two, three, four, five, and six: five atoms').
findings.recommended_outcome: The capstone worked example needs an atom enumeration a student can count along with and reach the stated number; the side-chain carbonyl carbon must be named as a ring member.

location.anchor_text: Alcohols are not normally eliminated by base: hydroxide is a poor leaving group

findings.observation: Within a single paragraph the chapter states that hydroxide is a poor leaving group and then, three sentences later, has the enolate 'eject hydroxide from the beta carbon'. Two sections later the Claisen text calls alkoxide 'a serviceable leaving group' with no explanation of why alkoxide is serviceable when hydroxide was poor — and no reminder of what a tetrahedral intermediate is or why collapsing it is favourable.
findings.learner_impact: Leaving-group ability is exactly the topic I am shakiest on. Being told a group is bad and then watching it leave, twice, in two different sections, with the word 'serviceable' doing all the explanatory work, is the point where I stop trying to reason and start memorising outcomes. From then on I answer every question in this chapter by pattern-matching, which is why I get ch23-claisen-product right and ch23-flawed-claisen wrong.
findings.evidence: blk-59t2y57n: 'hydroxide is a poor leaving group and there is no acidic proton to start from' followed by 'the enolate then pushes its electrons into the alpha-beta bond and ejects hydroxide from the beta carbon'. blk-6h9ci3tr: 'Alkoxide is a serviceable leaving group, the carbonyl reforms by expelling it'. Questions that depend on this: ch23-claisen-product (distractor b), ch23-flawed-claisen, ch23-addition-vs-dehydration-v2.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs to reconcile its own two statements about hydroxide/alkoxide leaving ability — a student must be able to see what makes expulsion possible in an E1cb and in a tetrahedral collapse when it is not possible in a plain alcohol.

location.anchor_text: The two reactions diverge at the tetrahedral intermediate.

findings.observation: All 26 assets in this chapter are static single-molecule renders of starting materials and isolated products. Not one intermediate is drawn anywhere: no tetrahedral intermediate, no alkoxide, no carbinolamine, no iminium ion, no enolate of the acceptor fragment, no curved arrow. The chapter's organising claim — that the aldol and the Claisen are the same reaction until the tetrahedral intermediate, at which point one is protonated and the other collapses — rests entirely on a species the student never sees.
findings.learner_impact: I cannot hold a four-species mechanism in words. When the chapter says 'the same intermediate carries an alkoxy group on the former carbonyl carbon', I have to build that structure in my head from a sentence while also tracking which molecule was donor and which was acceptor. I do not manage it. I then meet ch23-aldol-attack-arrow and ch23-michael-arrow, which ask me to place a curved arrow, and the chapter has never shown me a single curved arrow anywhere.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json assets[] — all 26 are plain molecule renders (mol-acetaldehyde through mol-wieland-miescher-ketone); the compiled reader contains 36 molecule blocks, 10 text blocks, 5 hidden video blocks and no reaction, reaction_coordinate, or mechanism block of any kind. Questions requiring the undrawn species: ch23-aldol-attack-arrow(+v2), ch23-michael-arrow(+v2), ch23-stork-route(+v2, intermediate m_iminium), ch23-claisen-product (distractor b reasoning), ch23-robinson-route (intermediate m_ketol).
findings.recommended_outcome: Students need to see the intermediates the chapter's central comparison turns on — at minimum the aldol alkoxide beside the Claisen tetrahedral intermediate, and the iminium the Stork sequence hydrolyses.

location.anchor_text: Two aldehydes, one new bond: the aldol reaction step by step

findings.observation: The package declares five step-by-step mechanism videos — video-aldol-mechanism, video-e1cb-dehydration, video-claisen-mechanism, video-conjugate-vs-direct-addition, video-robinson-two-stages — each with a written storyboard and learning goal. All five compile into the reader as video blocks with "url": "" and "is_hidden": true. The only media in the chapter designed to show motion through a mechanism is not delivered.
findings.learner_impact: These five are precisely the five things I would have watched instead of rereading: the aldol step sequence, why an alcohol eliminates in base, addition versus substitution at the tetrahedral intermediate, 1,2 versus 1,4 addition, and the two Robinson stages. Without them my only route into every mechanism is dense prose, which is the modality I am worst at. I reread the Michael section four times and still cannot say why a Grignard goes one place and a malonate anion another.
findings.evidence: Reader blocks blk-d5tojv1k, blk-anvkzdmx, blk-9d675oza, blk-awacta2q, blk-2cwyvg99 all carry "url": "" and "is_hidden": true. Their briefs in topic.package.json video_briefs[] are fully written (e.g. video-conjugate-vs-direct-addition: 'See the resonance forms that make an enone's beta carbon electrophilic, then watch a reactive nucleophile commit at the carbonyl carbon while a stabilized enolate reverses out').
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the promised step-through media must actually reach the reader, or each of those five mechanisms needs a delivered visual equivalent — the prose alone is not carrying them.

location.anchor_text: The profile below describes acetone being converted to a conjugated enone on warming with base.

findings.observation: Two advanced reaction_coordinate_reasoning questions ask for step count, rate-determining step, overall thermodynamics and per-step thermodynamics from a free-energy profile. The chapter contains no energy diagram of any kind and never uses the words transition state, activation barrier, rate-determining, exergonic, or endergonic in any of its ten sections at any detail level. The prose discusses equilibrium position and irreversibility in purely verbal terms ('sits far on the side of starting material', 'a one-way door').
findings.learner_impact: Reading a free-energy profile is a prior-chapter skill I never mastered, and this chapter builds no bridge to it — it does not even signal that I will need it. I meet a diagram cold, cannot remember whether the rate-determining step is the highest peak or the biggest climb, and guess. The hint ladder is good ('measure each climb from the valley immediately preceding it') but hints arrive after I have already decided I do not belong in this question.
findings.evidence: ch23-aldol-dehydration-profile and ch23-aldol-dehydration-profile-v2 ask ['step_count','rate_determining_step','overall','step_types']. Grepping the compiled reader for 'transition state', 'rate-determining', 'exergonic', 'endergonic', 'activation' returns nothing; the closest prose is 'Coupling an unfavorable equilibrium to a favorable irreversible step' in blk-59t2y57n.
findings.recommended_outcome: Before students are graded on a free-energy profile of these reactions, the chapter needs to connect its verbal equilibrium argument to a picture of the same argument — the coupled aldol/dehydration energetics are the natural place.

location.anchor_text: The mechanism has three steps and no surprises.

findings.observation: The aldol section states the mechanism has three steps (deprotonation, attack, protonation) and the dehydration section describes E1cb as two steps (deprotonation, expulsion). The reaction_coordinate_reasoning profile for the same overall transformation has step_count 2, with minima labelled 'Acetone (2 equivalents)', 'Aldol addition product', 'Conjugated enone + H₂O'. Nothing tells the student the profile is coarse-grained at the level of overall stages rather than elementary steps.
findings.learner_impact: I did the work. I memorised that the aldol has three steps. I look at a diagram of the aldol plus dehydration and the graded answer is two. Either my mechanism count was wrong or my diagram reading is wrong and I cannot tell which, so I lose confidence in the one fact I had actually learned. On the exam I now second-guess the three-step mechanism as well.

findings.recommended_outcome: The relationship between the mechanism's elementary steps and the stages a profile shows must be stated somewhere the student meets before being graded on it; a profile that lumps three steps into one hill needs to say so.

location.anchor_text: In a mixture of 2,2-dimethylpropanal, (CH₃)₃CCHO, and propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, which compound must serve as the donor, and why?

findings.observation: All ten nuggets carry a well-written practice_check with a prompt and a full worked answer.
